bull_thesis:
Everforth is a genuinely cash-generative technology-services business that is being valued as though its earnings are about to stop, and the second-quarter print of 29 July 2026 was the first hard evidence that they are not. Revenue of $1,007.0 million came with adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization - as a percentage of revenue) recovering from 8.6% in the March quarter to 9.6%, and adjusted earnings of $0.91 a share beat the $0.81 the street expected. That matters because the March-quarter margin miss was management's only real credibility wound, and their explanation for it - that record fourth-quarter bookings converted into revenue more slowly than the guide assumed, not that pricing broke - now has one quarter of support behind it.

Underneath the wobble the mix shift is real and measurable. Consulting work rose from 57% of revenue in early 2025 to about 63% by the end of the year, and the 2025 margin path tracked it almost exactly (9.7%, 10.6%, 11.1%, 11.0% across the four quarters). Commercial consulting bookings have run at a book-to-bill (new bookings divided by revenue) of 1.1 to 1.2 times on a trailing-twelve-month basis right through the worst of the client caution, including a record $444.4 million in the fourth quarter of 2025. The January 2026 purchase of Quinnox added India-based delivery centres running, on management's own description, gross margins in the low forties and profit margins 'in the twenties' - roughly double the parent's - plus a route to price work on outcomes rather than hours.

The cash is the anchor. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $221 million against an equity market value of about $1.33 billion, a free-cash-flow yield near 17%. The company converted roughly 55% of adjusted profit to free cash over the year, close to the 60% rule of thumb the CFO gave in April. It has used that cash to retire about 6% of its shares in a year (diluted count 44.0 million down to 41.2 million) under a $1 billion authorisation, and on 9 July 2026 it refinanced and upsized its revolving credit facility to $600 million, pushing the maturity from 2028 out to 2031 - so there is no near-term funding cliff to trip over. Insiders have been buying with their own money in the open market: 17 purchases of 96,375 shares against 11 sales of 39,663.

The federal side, about 30% of revenue, is the depressed half rather than the broken half. Backlog is still roughly $2.8 billion, about 2.4 times that segment's annual revenue, and the pressure came from an identifiable, dateable set of shocks - the DOGE cost-cutting programme, a lengthy government shutdown, and a Homeland Security leadership transition - against a defence budget that has just seen one of the largest single-year increases in modern history in areas (AI, cyber, cloud migration, secure communications) where this company actually competes. If federal award velocity normalises while commercial consulting keeps compounding, revenue stabilises around $4 billion and margin retraces toward the 11% the company printed as recently as the December 2025 quarter. On roughly $440 million of adjusted profit at an eight-times enterprise multiple, less $1.39 billion of net debt, that is a stock in the high forties to low fifties.

What has to hold: federal book-to-bill has to climb back above 1.0 from 0.7; commercial consulting has to keep converting bookings without another timing slip; and leverage has to come down through free cash flow rather than another debt-funded acquisition.
bear_thesis:
Strip out the transformation language and this is a business whose revenue peaked in 2022 at $4.58 billion and has fallen every year since, to $3.98 billion in 2025 and a trailing $3.97 billion now; whose earnings per share have fallen five years running, from $4.33 in 2021 to $2.60 in 2025 to $1.94 trailing; and whose return on invested capital is 7.7%, comfortably below any sensible cost of capital. A company earning below its cost of capital on a shrinking base is destroying value while it reorganises, and the rebrand does not change that arithmetic.

The most damaging number is one the company disclosed itself. Federal new-award book-to-bill decayed in a straight line across five quarters - 1.2 times, 1.1, 1.0, 0.9, then 0.7 by the March 2026 quarter - while backlog slid from $3.1 billion to about $2.8 billion. Roughly 30% of revenue is being fed by a pipeline that is filling more slowly than it empties, and government procurement is not a market you can fix with a sales incentive.

The balance sheet got worse precisely when it should have got better. Net debt (borrowings less cash) went from $1.008 billion at 31 December 2025 to $1.386 billion at 30 June 2026, funding the $283.6 million Quinnox purchase and roughly $50 million of buybacks in the first half, while trailing adjusted profit slipped from about $422 million to about $400 million. Leverage went from roughly 2.4 times profit to roughly 3.5 times in six months. Interest expense in the June quarter was $20.4 million, an $82 million annual run-rate, and it is rising into a bond market where the 30-year Treasury yield is 5.27%, the highest since 2007, with the Federal Reserve carrying a hiking bias. Shareholders' equity of $1.805 billion sits on $2.876 billion of goodwill and intangibles - tangible book value is roughly negative $1.07 billion, and the screener's solvency score of 1.8 sits in the distress band. Reported net income in the June quarter was $14.2 million, down 52% year on year; on the reported numbers this is a 16-times-earnings stock, not a 6-times one.

The structural worry is the one management has already conceded on the record. Their own artificial-intelligence accelerators complete discovery work '25% faster' and capture '40% more' of requirements - and, asked twice by analysts whether that changes what they charge, the answer was that pricing conversations are 'still early days' and that no uptick is being seen. Delivering the same outcome in fewer billable hours at unchanged rates is revenue deflation with a lag. That is the exact mechanism eating the information-technology services labour model, and it explains why comparable firms have de-rated as a cohort rather than one at a time.

Finally, the setup. The shares are $32.22, up about 91% from a $16.90 low set in July and 53% above their own 50-day average of $21.06, having re-rated on a single beat and, in the last week, on nothing at all. The Street is thin here - only two price targets printed last quarter - and the twelve-month average target has collapsed from $46.07 to a $32.80 consensus that is now level with the price. The catalyst has fired, the discount has closed, and the leverage, the federal bookings hole and the pricing question are all still unresolved. What would confirm the bear: a third consecutive quarter of federal book-to-bill below 1.0, adjusted margin failing to reach 10.5% by the December quarter, or any new debt-funded acquisition before leverage is back below 3 times.
consensus_delta:
For a deep-value name the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power. Our answer is: it was, in mid-July at $16.90; it largely is not any more at $32.22.

Where the Street is still demonstrably wrong is on the shape of its own coverage rather than the direction. Only two price targets printed in the last quarter - this is not a street-wide view, it is two analysts. The twelve-month average target has collapsed from $46.07 to a $32.80 consensus, and target velocity is running 37% below the year-ago average, which tells you the sell side marked the stock down after the fact and is now anchored to a price the shares have already reached. The most recent target, Tobey Sommer's $36.00 on 22 July 2026, was set when the stock was $18.31 - it was a 97% upside call then and it is a 12% upside call now, unchanged. Surinder Thind's $22.00 from 29 May was set at $20.90. In other words, nobody's published view has been refreshed for either the second-quarter beat or the doubling. The consensus is stale in both directions and should not be treated as an anchor.

Where we disagree with the bulls: the market is now extrapolating one margin quarter (8.6% to 9.6%) into a return to the 11% the company printed in December, and is doing so while the federal segment's trailing book-to-bill sits at 0.7 times and its backlog is down about 10% year on year. Roughly 30% of revenue is being fed by a shrinking pipeline, and no amount of commercial consulting momentum fixes a government procurement gap on a two-quarter view.

Where we disagree with the bears: the 'melting ice cube' read is too harsh. This company generated $221 million of free cash flow over the last twelve months, converts roughly 55% of adjusted profit to cash, has refinanced its revolver out to 2031, has retired about 6% of its shares in a year, and has insiders buying in the open market. That is not the cash-flow signature of terminal decline. The honest position is in the middle, and the middle is roughly where the price now sits.
forcing_function:
For this name the question is what event forces the market to re-rate a stable-earning business - and the honest answer is that the one available forcing function has already fired. The 29 July 2026 second-quarter result was it: the margin inflection landed, the beat was reported, and the stock has re-rated about 91% off its July low.

What remains dated and observable: the third-quarter print in late October 2026, which is a verification event rather than a re-rating event - it either confirms the margin path toward 11% and the federal bookings recovery, or it breaks the recovery narrative. Watch two disclosures specifically: federal book-to-bill on a trailing basis (needs to cross back above 1.0 from 0.7) and adjusted margin (needs 10.5% or better to keep the recovery credible).

The structural forcing functions that would re-rate this materially higher are all discretionary and undated. The $1 billion repurchase authorisation is the strongest lever the company controls - with roughly 41 million shares outstanding and a $1.33 billion market value, that authorisation is theoretically most of the company, and if free cash flow were redirected to it rather than to acquisitions the share count could shrink meaningfully. But management has just demonstrated the opposite preference by spending $283.6 million on Quinnox and slowing the buyback to $11.5 million in the June quarter. There is no activist on the register that we can source, no announced strategic review and no asset sale. A separation of the federal business - where the peer multiple is roughly 1.1 times revenue against the 0.65-0.80 the commercial market commands - is the theoretical value-unlocking event, and nothing in the record suggests it is contemplated.

So: one spent catalyst, one dated verification point in late October, and no live corporate event. Per this book's rule that a spent catalyst is neither rewarded nor penalised, this does not push the score either way - it simply means there is nothing scheduled to rescue a position bought at the wrong price.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry three specific hazards, none of them a liquidity event.

First, the third-quarter print in late October 2026 is a high bar into a stock that has doubled. The comparison is a quarter in which the company earned an 11.1% adjusted margin on $1,011 million of revenue. Anything short of continued sequential margin progress - and the company has told us the recovery will be gradual and 'won't rubber band' - lands on a shareholder base that bought the re-rate, not the discount. This is the most likely source of a violent give-back.

Second, the federal segment. Award velocity has been suppressed by the DOGE cost-cutting programme, a lengthy government shutdown and a Homeland Security leadership transition. If book-to-bill prints below 1.0 for a third consecutive quarter, the $2.8 billion backlog starts converting into visibly declining segment revenue in 2027 rather than a recovery, and the 0.90-times-revenue multiple we pay for that segment in the base case is too generous.

Third, the cost of the balance sheet. Interest expense ran at $20.4 million in the June quarter, an $82 million annual rate, and it is rising - net debt went from $1.008 billion to $1.386 billion in six months to fund the Quinnox purchase and buybacks. Leverage is about 3.5 times adjusted profit. The macro backdrop is hostile to that: the 30-year Treasury yield is 5.27%, the highest since 2007, the Federal Reserve held on 28-29 July with all three dissents voting FOR a hike, and roughly 57-65% odds of a September hike are priced with no cuts through December. Crucially, this thesis contains no rate-rescue leg and needs none - the revolver was refinanced and upsized to $600 million on 9 July 2026 with maturity pushed to 2031, so there is no wall to refinance into the storm. But every additional turn of leverage is now more expensive, and the first-half pattern of debt-funded acquisition plus buyback cannot repeat without impairing the equity.

What is NOT a hazard: cash burn. Free cash flow is positive and covers interest roughly 2.7 times.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic to exploit here, and that is part of why we are not paying up. The company pays no dividend, so there is no yield-focused holder base to flush on a cut. There is no index event: the shares remain a small-cap NYSE listing with no announced addition or deletion. There is no lock-up, no spin-off distribution and no announced secondary.

The flow that actually moved this stock ran the other way. The shares bottomed at $16.90 in July - roughly 69% below the 52-week high of $54.94 - which is the signature of a genuine capitulation in a thinly-covered small cap that had missed on margin, lost its federal bookings momentum and re-branded mid-stumble. That washout has already been harvested by whoever bought it. Since then the marginal buyer has been momentum and screen-driven: quantitative 'strong buy' value lists picked the name up on 31 July and again on 5 and 10 August, and the last week's 13% move came with no company news at all. The company itself has been buying, but at a decelerating pace - $46.0 million of repurchases in the September 2025 quarter, $64.2 million in December, $39.0 million in March, and only $11.5 million in June as cash went to the acquisition and to paying down borrowings. The corporate bid is thinner now than at any point in the last year, precisely when the price is highest.

The practical read: the shareholder base that would panic has already panicked, and the buyers who replaced it are price-insensitive on the way in and will be price-insensitive on the way out. A disappointing October print into a screen-driven holder base is a fast reversal, not an orderly de-rating.
moderator_conclusion:
We are continuing coverage, not opening it, and our call is unchanged: wait for the wash-out. A week ago at $28.44 we put base-case fair value at $36 and said the tension was that the market had already paid for the first proof point. The shares have since added another 13%, to $32.22, on no company news - an AWS partner-tier press release and two quantitative 'strong buy' list additions do not move intrinsic value. So the thesis is intact and the price has eaten most of it.

What we own an opinion on. Everforth is a real, cash-generative technology-services franchise, roughly 70% commercial and 30% federal, that has done genuine work converting itself from selling billable hours to selling delivered outcomes - consulting rose from 57% to about 63% of revenue and the 2025 margin path followed it up to 11%. The second-quarter print of 29 July confirmed the margin inflection was timing rather than breakage, with adjusted profit margin back to 9.6% and an earnings beat. Trailing free cash flow of $221 million against a $1.33 billion market value is a 17% yield, the revolver has been refinanced out to 2031, roughly 6% of the shares have been retired in a year, and insiders are buying in the open market. None of that is the signature of a business in terminal decline.

What stops us paying today's price. Three things, in order. First, the sum-of-the-parts arithmetic: on peer multiples we pulled live this morning, the parts come to about $36 in the base case, $22 in the adverse case and $50 in the favorable case. At $32.22 there is roughly ten dollars of downside against under four dollars of upside to fair value - the inverse of the setup we underwrote last week. Second, the leverage: net debt went from $1.008 billion to $1.386 billion in six months to fund an acquisition and buybacks while profit slipped, taking leverage from about 2.4 to about 3.5 times. Because debt is more than half of enterprise value, the equity absorbs the full force of any multiple compression - a 20% cut to the operating multiple takes roughly 40% off the share price. Third, and structurally, the federal segment's new-award book-to-bill has decayed for five straight quarters to 0.7 times with backlog down about 10%, and management has conceded on the record that its own artificial-intelligence accelerators complete work materially faster without any change in what it charges. Fewer billable hours at unchanged rates is revenue deflation with a lag, and it is why the whole commercial technology-services cohort has de-rated together. Everforth's 6.8 times profit is roughly in line with EPAM's 6.5 - the discount is sector-wide repricing, not a single-name mispricing, and we refuse to book shared sector beta as edge.

On the market backdrop: the current regime rewards catalysts with a calendar date and a cash payoff and penalises theses that need cheaper money. This one needs neither - the revolver is refinanced to 2031 and the thesis has no rate-cut leg, which is a genuine mark in its favour in a tape where the Federal Reserve is carrying a hiking bias and the 30-year yield is the highest since 2007. But it also has no live dated driver: the catalyst fired on 29 July, and the next scheduled event is a verification print in late October that is a hurdle, not a rescue.

On the two scores. Our execution call is 'wait', conviction 3 - the level we are waiting for is $26 or better, which restores roughly two dollars of upside for every dollar of risk against the same $36 base case; alternatively, we would move without a price concession on a single dated fact - federal trailing book-to-bill printing back above 1.0 in the October report. Separately, judging the value case alone with no catalyst overlay and no regime tilt: a business earning a 7.7% return on invested capital, below its cost of capital, with revenue down five consecutive years and earnings per share compounding down 12% a year, carries an eroding moat by this committee's own definition - and an eroding moat caps the value score at 3 regardless of the optical cheapness. With the discount to fair value now around a tenth, 3 is where it lands on its own merits anyway. A low multiple on a base that is shrinking is not value; it becomes value again at a price that pays us for the shrinkage, and $32.22 is not that price.
sop_breakdown:
Base case, built from the two reported segments and blended peer multiples that sit between the adverse and favorable cases: Commercial Business $2.79 billion of revenue at 0.65 times = $1.81 billion; Federal Government Business $1.19 billion at 0.90 times = $1.07 billion; enterprise value $2.89 billion; less net debt of $1.386 billion (30 June 2026 balance sheet: borrowings $1.438 billion minus cash $52 million, the ex-lease definition, with no capitalised leases on the sheet); equity $1.50 billion across 41.2 million diluted shares = about $36 a share.

Sanity checks. That implies roughly 7.2 times trailing adjusted profit of about $400 million on an enterprise basis and about 0.73 times revenue - against EPAM at 6.5 times profit and 0.79 times revenue, Genpact at 7.5 and 1.27, SAIC at 10.8 and 1.09, Booz Allen at 10.2 and 1.15. So the base case asks the market to pay a commercial-services multiple for the whole company and gives no credit at all for the federal half being valued like a government-services firm. It also implies about 15 times trailing free cash flow of $221 million on the enterprise, or roughly 6.7 times free cash flow on the equity - undemanding.

One data caveat, stated rather than buried: the cash-flow statement's period-end cash of $152.9 million does not reconcile to the balance sheet's $52.2 million. We have used the balance-sheet figure, which is the more conservative. If the larger cash balance is correct, net debt is nearer $1.29 billion and every figure in this stack is about $2.40 a share higher.
risk_reward: Unattractive at $32.22. The adverse case sits at $22 and the base case at $36, so the shares are about $10 below the downside and less than $4 below fair value - roughly three dollars of risk for every dollar of reward, the inverse of the setup we underwrote a week ago at $28.44. The favorable case at $50 is the only leg that pays, and it needs federal bookings to recover and margin to return to 11% - neither of which is in evidence yet. There is no structural floor to lean on: net debt of $1.386 billion is more than half of enterprise value, so the equity takes the full leverage of any multiple compression. Note also the pipeline computes these ratios from the point numbers - we state levels only.
peer_comps_note:
The supplied peer file for this ticker came back unmapped - it declined to identify the company and offered no peer set or anchor multiple. Rather than reason from memory, we pulled live trailing multiples on 10 August 2026 and built the comparison ourselves. Federal government services: CACI 17.7 times enterprise value to adjusted profit and 2.03 times revenue; ICF International 12.9 and 1.24; SAIC 10.8 and 1.09; Booz Allen 10.2 and 1.15. Commercial technology services: Genpact 7.5 and 1.27; EPAM 6.5 and 0.79; Kforce 0.88 times revenue (its 20.5 times profit multiple is a trough-earnings artifact and we ignore it); DXC 2.6 and 0.32 as the structurally-declining anchor at the bottom.

Everforth trades at 6.8 times trailing adjusted profit and 0.68 times revenue on the whole company. Against the commercial cohort that is roughly in line, not cheap - EPAM at 6.5 times is the honest read-across, and EPAM is net cash while Everforth carries 3.5 times leverage. The apparent bargain comes entirely from applying government-services multiples to the 30% federal slice. Two cautions follow. First, the commercial cohort's de-rating is a shared sector move on the same unresolved driver - whether artificial intelligence deflates hours-based services revenue - so the gap to the federal names is sector beta, not name-specific edge, and we do not credit it as alpha. Second, Everforth's own federal slice has a 0.7 times book-to-bill against peers whose award momentum is intact, which is why our base case pays only 0.90 times revenue for it rather than the 1.09-1.15 the peers command.
interrogator_dossier:
# Everforth, Inc. (NYSE: EFOR, formerly ASGN) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 2026-08-10. Transcript evidence: five consecutive quarterly calls, 2025-04-23 through 2026-04-22 (the company's first-quarter 2026 call was its last under the ASGN name). The 2026-07-29 second-quarter call is NOT in the transcript bundle; where I use second-quarter figures they come from the company's own results release of 29 July 2026 and from the filed statements, and I say so.*

*Price used throughout: $32.22 per share (US dollars, New York Stock Exchange), the live quote on 2026-08-10.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has changed shape three times in five quarters, and each shift moved the burden of proof further out in time.

**Spring 2025 — "resilience".** The first-quarter 2025 call is defensive in posture but calm in tone. Revenue of $968.3 million and an adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, as a percentage of revenue) of 9.7% were "in line with our guidance". The framing was stabilizers: "our business model demonstrates resilience across economic cycles, primarily due to our business stabilizers that support our gross margin, along with our variable cost structure." Two external shocks were named and quantified — tariffs and the federal cost-cutting programme known as DOGE. Management widened its guidance range and said so plainly: "there's a new piece of news almost daily here that all of our clients are reacting to."

**Mid-2025 to early 2026 — "mix shift".** Through the second, third and fourth quarters of 2025 the narrative turned offensive and settled on a single measurable claim: the company is converting itself from an information-technology staffing business into a consulting and solutions business. Consulting revenue rose from 57% of the total in early 2025 to roughly 63% by the fourth quarter. Adjusted margin climbed with it — 10.6%, then 11.1%, then 11.0%. Two acquisitions (TopBloc, a Workday services specialist, closed March 2025; Quinnox, an India-based digital-engineering firm, announced January 2026) were presented as the accelerant, alongside a $1 billion share-repurchase authorisation. This is the strongest stretch of the record: the claim was specific, the numbers moved with it, and management put capital behind it.

**Spring 2026 — "transformation, with a stumble".** The first-quarter 2026 call carries the rebrand to Everforth, a new stock ticker, a re-cut of segment reporting (from mode of delivery to industry vertical), three new segment presidents, and the closing of Quinnox. It also carries the first plain admission of a miss: "adjusted EBITDA margin of 8.6% was below our expectations for the quarter." Note what happened to the reporting change and the miss in the same call — the company stopped disclosing the staffing-versus-consulting split at exactly the moment its economics wobbled. The stated reason ("the delivery structure of our engagement is much less meaningful than the outcomes we drive") is defensible on the merits and convenient in its timing.

**Quietly dropped along the way:** the "business stabilizers" language of early 2025; the specific federal revenue baseline Ted Hanson volunteered in July 2025 ("mid $290 million to mid $295 million" per quarter); and, in the 2026 reporting change, the assignment-versus-consulting revenue disclosure that had been the transformation's own scoreboard.

**Newly introduced:** offshore delivery in India as a structural cost lever (Quinnox), proprietary artificial-intelligence "accelerators" as a differentiator, and the H-1B visa policy change reframed as "an incremental positive."

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our IT consulting revenues continue to grow… approximately 63% of revenues" | Q2–Q4 2025 | Consistent with a rising adjusted margin through 2025 (9.7% → 10.6% → 11.1% → 11.0%). But total revenue still fell: $4.45B (2023) → $4.10B (2024) → $3.98B (2025). | **Half true.** The mix is genuinely shifting; it has not yet arrested the top line. |
| "We're continuing to see our margins here kind of be creeping up" (on AI investment) | Q2 2025 | True through Q4 2025, then reversed: 8.6% in Q1 2026, 9.6% in Q2 2026 — both below the 2025 exit rate of 11.0%. | **Did not hold.** |
| "Our margins… it's not degrading, it's adding to our margin profile" | Q2 2025 | Net profit margin is 2.9% and earnings per share fell for the fifth consecutive year: $4.33 (2021) → $2.60 (2025), a five-year compound decline of about 12% a year. Trailing-twelve-month earnings per share are now $1.94. | **Contradicted by the trajectory.** |
| Federal business "positioned strongly for the future" on defence-budget growth | Q2–Q4 2025 | Federal new-award momentum decayed every quarter: book-to-bill (new bookings divided by revenue) on a trailing-twelve-month basis went 1.2x → 1.1x → 1.0x → 0.9x → **0.7x** by Q1 2026. Backlog fell from $3.1B to about $2.8B. | **Refuted by the company's own disclosure.** This is the single most damaging number in the record. |
| "Disciplined approach to capital allocation… without compromising the strength of our balance sheet" | Q4 2025 | Net debt (borrowings less cash) went from $1.008B at 31 Dec 2025 to $1.386B at 30 June 2026 — funding the $283.6M Quinnox purchase and roughly $50M of buybacks in the first half — while trailing adjusted profit fell from about $422M to about $400M. Leverage rose from roughly 2.4x to roughly **3.5x** in six months. | **Materially overstated.** Balance-sheet strength was spent, not preserved. |
| "We're not seeing a material compression in pricing" | Q1 2026 | Gross margin is stable (28.9%, and 28.3% in Q2 2026 versus 28.7% a year earlier). So the pricing claim survives; the damage is below the gross line — operating leverage, not price. | **Holds.** |
| Free cash flow "60% of our adjusted EBITDA converting" | Q1 2026 | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $221M on roughly $400M of adjusted profit — about 55%, close to the rule of thumb. | **Broadly holds.** |

The pattern: everything management says about *mix* and *cash conversion* checks out; everything it says about *the durability of margin and the balance sheet* has been overtaken by events.

One more forensic point the calls never surface. Shareholders' equity of $1.805B sits on top of $2.280B of goodwill and $0.596B of other intangible assets — tangible book value is roughly **negative $1.07B**. The screener's Altman-Z solvency score of 1.8 sits in the distress band. Neither is fatal for an asset-light services firm with $221M of free cash flow, but it means the equity is a claim on contracts and people, not on assets, and the debt is senior to all of it.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining, with a late partial recovery.**

- **Q1 2025 — cautious but composed.** "It's just the right thing to do here to widen the range." Management named its uncertainties and sized them ("we only expanded the range by $10 million on the top").
- **Q2 2025 — the high-water mark.** "Revenues of $1.02 billion were above the high-end of our guidance range." Confident, specific, forward-leaning: "we've got things developing here… we're on a path here that I think that we're going to be in a good spot."
- **Q3 2025 — confident, but the language turns abstract.** Heavy use of third-party validation (the ISG index) rather than first-party commitments: "AI spending is not merely a passing fad but a fundamental replatforming."
- **Q4 2025 — promotional.** The rebrand, the acquisition, the $1 billion authorisation and the Investor Day all arrive together. Superlatives multiply ("acquirer of choice", "record bookings").
- **Q1 2026 — the tone breaks.** "Below our expectations." Sales cycles "getting slightly longer as clients are deliberating longer before they pull the trigger." And the telling hedge, twice: "we will see the recovery in margin gradually throughout the year, won't rubber band it." When a management team pre-emptively tells you the recovery will be slow, it is managing an expectation it no longer controls.

The shift from offensive to defensive vocabulary is measurable: 2025 calls lead with bookings, wins and mix; the 2026 call leads with "disciplined expense management", "variability" and "volatile macro environment."

The 29 July 2026 second-quarter release (not in the transcript bundle) partially reverses this: adjusted earnings of $0.91 per share beat the $0.81 consensus, and adjusted margin recovered from 8.6% to 9.6%. But revenue of $1,007.0 million was still down about 1.3% from a year earlier, and reported net income of $14.2 million was down 52%.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.**

Tracking each guide to its outcome:

| Guided in | For | Delivered | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025 (widened range) | Q2 2025 | $1.02B revenue "above the high-end"; margin 10.6% "at the top end" | Over-delivered |
| Q2 2025 | Q3 2025 | $1.01B and 11.1% — "both at the high end of our guidance ranges" | Delivered |
| Q3 2025 | Q4 2025 | $980.1M "at the top end"; 11.0% "exceeding our expectation" | Delivered |
| Q4 2025 | Q1 2026 | Revenue in range; **margin 8.6%, below expectations** | Missed |
| Q1 2026 | Q2 2026 | Revenue $1,007.0M; margin 9.6%; adjusted earnings $0.91 vs $0.81 expected | Beat |

That is a genuinely good record on revenue and a mixed one on margin. Two things stop it earning a High score.

First, the widened range of early 2025 was a lowered bar, and three "top of the range" quarters were cleared against it — the screener's beat rate of four in seven quarters (57%) is the unflattering long-run version. Second, and more importantly, the Q1 2026 miss came *directly after* record fourth-quarter bookings, and management's explanation was conversion timing: "our guide for Q1 assumed historical conversion of those things… the ramp-up time for those projects was slower than anticipated." A company that cannot forecast the conversion of its own signed backlog one quarter out has a real forecasting problem, not a macro problem.

No sandbagging pattern is evident; if anything the Q1 2026 guide was set too optimistically off the bookings number.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The margin run-rate.** Surinder Thind has pressed on it every call. In Q1 2025 he extracted a direct commitment — "so 2Q should be kind of the average run rate going forward… ?" and CFO Marie Perry answered "Yes." Margin has since ranged from 8.6% to 11.1%. In Q3 2025 he pushed again on the federal cost-reimbursable mix and got a deflection ("just the natural ebb and flow of certain contracts ending").

**The pricing of AI productivity — the question management keeps not answering.** In Q3 2025 Maggie Nolan asked whether accelerators that deliver work "25% faster" trigger a pricing conversation. Shiv Iyer: "We are exploring those opportunities, but we're not seeing a big uptick today." In Q1 2026 Mark Marcon asked the same question from the other side and got "we're not seeing a material compression in pricing." Both answers can be true at once and together they describe the core economic risk: the company is delivering the same outcome with fewer billable hours and is not being paid for the efficiency. In a business that sells hours, that is revenue deflation with a lag.

**Federal award velocity.** Analysts asked about DOGE's effect on decision-making from Q1 2025 onward. Rand Blazer's answer — "that velocity is less visible to us… of course, that's where we wouldn't be privy to that at any rate" — was honest and, in hindsight, a warning. The book-to-bill decay to 0.7x is that warning arriving.

**Not being asked, and it should be:** how a company adding leverage to buy growth (Quinnox) and to buy its own stock reconciles that with a shrinking federal backlog and a margin that has not returned to its 2025 exit rate.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Federal new-award collapse.** Trailing book-to-bill 1.2x (Q1 2025) → 0.7x (Q1 2026); backlog $3.1B → $2.8B. Roughly 30% of revenue is being fed by a shrinking pipeline.

🔴 **Leverage bought with a falling profit base.** Net debt $1.008B → $1.386B in six months while trailing adjusted profit slipped; leverage roughly 2.4x → 3.5x. Interest expense is now running at about $82M a year annualised from the second quarter.

🔴 **Five straight years of falling earnings.** $4.33 (2021) → $2.60 (2025) → $1.94 trailing. Revenue peaked in 2022 at $4.58B.

🔴 **Disclosure narrowed at the moment of the stumble** (Q1 2026): the staffing-versus-consulting split was retired in the same call that reported the first margin miss.

🔴 **Bookings that do not convert on schedule** (Q1 2026), following "record" fourth-quarter bookings (Q4 2025) — the transformation's own scoreboard proved a poor leading indicator.

🟢 **The mix shift is real and margin-accretive.** Consulting 57% → 63% of revenue; the 2025 margin path (9.7% → 11.0%) tracked it.

🟢 **Cash generation holds through the downturn.** $221M of trailing free cash flow on a $1.33B equity market value; conversion near the 60%-of-adjusted-profit rule of thumb.

🟢 **Second-quarter 2026 margin inflection** (29 July 2026): 8.6% → 9.6%, with an earnings beat — the first evidence the Q1 stumble was timing, as management claimed.

🟢 **Financing risk pushed out.** On 9 July 2026 the company refinanced and upsized its revolving credit facility to $600 million, extending maturity from 2028 to 2031. There is no near-term maturity wall.

🟢 **Shares are actually being retired.** Diluted share count 44.0M (Q1 2025) → 41.2M (Q2 2026), about 6% in a year, against a $1 billion authorisation.

🟢 **Insiders buying with their own money.** Open-market activity of 17 purchases (96,375 shares) against 11 sales (39,663 shares).

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Assets and accelerators" replaced "resources".** Across 2025 the unit of value being sold shifts in management's own vocabulary from people to intellectual property. Iyer floats productising it — "we have something called Pathfinder, which is an AI-driven cybersecurity product… conversations about pricing differently. But those are still early days" (Q3 2025). Early days, still, three quarters later.

**Offshore became strategy, not supplement.** In Q4 2025 Quinnox's India centres are described as "the foundation of our offshore delivery platform" with "EBITDA margins in the twenties" — roughly double the parent's. Management is buying the cost structure it cannot build. That is rational, and it is also an admission about the economics of the legacy base.

**Three new segment presidents in one quarter** (Q1 2026: Commercial North America, India and International, Federal Government). A wholesale operating-leadership replacement alongside a rebrand is a bigger vote of no confidence in the prior structure than the calm narration suggests.

**Competitive framing softened.** In Q3 2025 Iyer names the competitive set — "a combination of Accenture or the Big Four, in some cases, the India-based pure plays" — and insists "we're seeing pricing… really hold up." By Q1 2026 the competitive discussion has disappeared, replaced by client-deliberation language.

**A quiet compensation tell.** Asked in Q1 2026 whether sales incentives are being restructured for the consulting pivot, Ted Hanson describes "a normal amount of change" and Iyer adds "a core tenet of that plan hasn't shifted." A company genuinely re-engineering what it sells usually re-engineers how it pays for selling.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** This is not a stable compounder and it is not yet a broken business. It is a mid-cap technology-services firm midway through a deliberate conversion from selling billable hours to selling delivered outcomes — with a real, measurable mix shift behind it, and a shrinking revenue base, a compressed margin and a leveraged balance sheet in front of it.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** The federal segment, roughly 30% of revenue, has a trailing book-to-bill of 0.7x and a backlog down about 10% year on year. Everything bullish about this company rests on the commercial consulting side compounding fast enough to outrun that. Size the position to the possibility that it does not — and note that the entry price has already moved: the shares are $32.22 today against a low of $16.90 within the last year and a 50-day average of $21.06.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is genuine but thin — switching costs on multi-year engagements and embedded client relationships on the commercial side, plus a regulatory-licence element on the federal side (security clearances, contract vehicles, a $2.8B backlog that competitors cannot bid into mid-term). The evidence forces the "eroding" label rather than "narrow but stable": return on invested capital is 7.7%, below any plausible cost of capital, and falling; return on equity 12.8%; net margin 2.9%; the screener puts the current margin 2.5 standard deviations below its own historical peak; and earnings per share have compounded *down* 12% a year for five years. A business earning below its cost of capital on a shrinking revenue base does not have a widening moat, whatever the mix shift says.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The force is the automation of information-technology services labour — artificial intelligence decoupling revenue from headcount in a business model that bills hours at a spread. Management has already conceded the mechanism on the record: accelerators deliver discovery "25% faster" and capture "40% more" of requirements, and pricing has not changed to capture it. Fewer hours at unchanged rates is deflation. Two things keep it short of terminal. First, the federal 30% is protected by clearances and procurement friction that AI does not dissolve. Second, the company is on the delivering side of the same wave — the demand for the cloud, data and platform work that makes enterprise AI possible is real and is what carried the commercial book-to-bill at 1.1–1.2x through the downturn.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Neither cleanly, and that is the honest answer. At $32.22 the shares are about 6.0 times trailing free cash flow of $221M on the equity, and the whole enterprise (equity plus $1.386B of net debt) is about 6.8 times trailing adjusted profit — cheap in absolute terms and roughly *in line with*, not at a discount to, where the market now prices comparable commercial technology-services firms after their own de-rating. The cheapness is substantially a sector repricing, not a single-name mispricing. What tips it away from being a trap is the cash: $221M of annual free cash flow against a $1.33B market value, a refinanced revolver running to 2031, a shrinking share count and insiders buying. What keeps it away from being a bargain is the leverage at 3.5 times profit, the federal bookings hole, and the fact that the shares have already nearly doubled off the July low before any of it is proven.

---

bull_thesis:
Everforth is a genuinely cash-generative technology-services business that is being valued as though its earnings are about to stop, and the second-quarter print of 29 July 2026 was the first hard evidence that they are not. Revenue of $1,007.0 million came with adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization - as a percentage of revenue) recovering from 8.6% in the March quarter to 9.6%, and adjusted earnings of $0.91 a share beat the $0.81 the street expected. That matters because the March-quarter margin miss was management's only real credibility wound, and their explanation for it - that record fourth-quarter bookings converted into revenue more slowly than the guide assumed, not that pricing broke - now has one quarter of support behind it.

Underneath the wobble the mix shift is real and measurable. Consulting work rose from 57% of revenue in early 2025 to about 63% by the end of the year, and the 2025 margin path tracked it almost exactly (9.7%, 10.6%, 11.1%, 11.0% across the four quarters). Commercial consulting bookings have run at a book-to-bill (new bookings divided by revenue) of 1.1 to 1.2 times on a trailing-twelve-month basis right through the worst of the client caution, including a record $444.4 million in the fourth quarter of 2025. The January 2026 purchase of Quinnox added India-based delivery centres running, on management's own description, gross margins in the low forties and profit margins 'in the twenties' - roughly double the parent's - plus a route to price work on outcomes rather than hours.

The cash is the anchor. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $221 million against an equity market value of about $1.33 billion, a free-cash-flow yield near 17%. The company converted roughly 55% of adjusted profit to free cash over the year, close to the 60% rule of thumb the CFO gave in April. It has used that cash to retire about 6% of its shares in a year (diluted count 44.0 million down to 41.2 million) under a $1 billion authorisation, and on 9 July 2026 it refinanced and upsized its revolving credit facility to $600 million, pushing the maturity from 2028 out to 2031 - so there is no near-term funding cliff to trip over. Insiders have been buying with their own money in the open market: 17 purchases of 96,375 shares against 11 sales of 39,663.

The federal side, about 30% of revenue, is the depressed half rather than the broken half. Backlog is still roughly $2.8 billion, about 2.4 times that segment's annual revenue, and the pressure came from an identifiable, dateable set of shocks - the DOGE cost-cutting programme, a lengthy government shutdown, and a Homeland Security leadership transition - against a defence budget that has just seen one of the largest single-year increases in modern history in areas (AI, cyber, cloud migration, secure communications) where this company actually competes. If federal award velocity normalises while commercial consulting keeps compounding, revenue stabilises around $4 billion and margin retraces toward the 11% the company printed as recently as the December 2025 quarter. On roughly $440 million of adjusted profit at an eight-times enterprise multiple, less $1.39 billion of net debt, that is a stock in the high forties to low fifties.

What has to hold: federal book-to-bill has to climb back above 1.0 from 0.7; commercial consulting has to keep converting bookings without another timing slip; and leverage has to come down through free cash flow rather than another debt-funded acquisition.
bear_thesis:
Strip out the transformation language and this is a business whose revenue peaked in 2022 at $4.58 billion and has fallen every year since, to $3.98 billion in 2025 and a trailing $3.97 billion now; whose earnings per share have fallen five years running, from $4.33 in 2021 to $2.60 in 2025 to $1.94 trailing; and whose return on invested capital is 7.7%, comfortably below any sensible cost of capital. A company earning below its cost of capital on a shrinking base is destroying value while it reorganises, and the rebrand does not change that arithmetic.

The most damaging number is one the company disclosed itself. Federal new-award book-to-bill decayed in a straight line across five quarters - 1.2 times, 1.1, 1.0, 0.9, then 0.7 by the March 2026 quarter - while backlog slid from $3.1 billion to about $2.8 billion. Roughly 30% of revenue is being fed by a pipeline that is filling more slowly than it empties, and government procurement is not a market you can fix with a sales incentive.

The balance sheet got worse precisely when it should have got better. Net debt (borrowings less cash) went from $1.008 billion at 31 December 2025 to $1.386 billion at 30 June 2026, funding the $283.6 million Quinnox purchase and roughly $50 million of buybacks in the first half, while trailing adjusted profit slipped from about $422 million to about $400 million. Leverage went from roughly 2.4 times profit to roughly 3.5 times in six months. Interest expense in the June quarter was $20.4 million, an $82 million annual run-rate, and it is rising into a bond market where the 30-year Treasury yield is 5.27%, the highest since 2007, with the Federal Reserve carrying a hiking bias. Shareholders' equity of $1.805 billion sits on $2.876 billion of goodwill and intangibles - tangible book value is roughly negative $1.07 billion, and the screener's solvency score of 1.8 sits in the distress band. Reported net income in the June quarter was $14.2 million, down 52% year on year; on the reported numbers this is a 16-times-earnings stock, not a 6-times one.

The structural worry is the one management has already conceded on the record. Their own artificial-intelligence accelerators complete discovery work '25% faster' and capture '40% more' of requirements - and, asked twice by analysts whether that changes what they charge, the answer was that pricing conversations are 'still early days' and that no uptick is being seen. Delivering the same outcome in fewer billable hours at unchanged rates is revenue deflation with a lag. That is the exact mechanism eating the information-technology services labour model, and it explains why comparable firms have de-rated as a cohort rather than one at a time.

Finally, the setup. The shares are $32.22, up about 91% from a $16.90 low set in July and 53% above their own 50-day average of $21.06, having re-rated on a single beat and, in the last week, on nothing at all. What would confirm the bear: a third consecutive quarter of federal book-to-bill below 1.0, adjusted margin failing to reach 10.5% by the December quarter, or any new debt-funded acquisition before leverage is back below 3 times.

forcing_function:
For this name the question is what event forces the market to re-rate a stable-earning business - and the honest answer is that the one available forcing function has already fired. The 29 July 2026 second-quarter result was it: the margin inflection landed, the beat was reported, and the stock has re-rated about 91% off its July low.

What remains dated and observable: the third-quarter print in late October 2026, which is a verification event rather than a re-rating event - it either confirms the margin path toward 11% and the federal bookings recovery, or it breaks the recovery narrative. Watch two disclosures specifically: federal book-to-bill on a trailing basis (needs to cross back above 1.0 from 0.7) and adjusted margin (needs 10.5% or better to keep the recovery credible).

The structural forcing functions that would re-rate this materially higher are all discretionary and undated. The $1 billion repurchase authorisation is the strongest lever the company controls - with roughly 41 million shares outstanding and a $1.33 billion market value, that authorisation is theoretically most of the company, and if free cash flow were redirected to it rather than to acquisitions the share count could shrink meaningfully. But management has just demonstrated the opposite preference by spending $283.6 million on Quinnox and slowing the buyback to $11.5 million in the June quarter. There is no activist on the register that we can source, no announced strategic review and no asset sale. A separation of the federal business - where the peer multiple is roughly 1.1 times revenue against the 0.65-0.80 the commercial market commands - is the theoretical value-unlocking event, and nothing in the record suggests it is contemplated.

So: one spent catalyst, one dated verification point in late October, and no live corporate event. Per this book's rule that a spent catalyst is neither rewarded nor penalised, this does not push the score either way - it simply means there is nothing scheduled to rescue a position bought at the wrong price.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months carry three specific hazards, none of them a liquidity event.

First, the third-quarter print in late October 2026 is a high bar into a stock that has doubled. The comparison is a quarter in which the company earned an 11.1% adjusted margin on $1,011 million of revenue. Anything short of continued sequential margin progress - and the company has told us the recovery will be gradual and 'won't rubber band' - lands on a shareholder base that bought the re-rate, not the discount. This is the most likely source of a violent give-back.

Second, the federal segment. Award velocity has been suppressed by the DOGE cost-cutting programme, a lengthy government shutdown and a Homeland Security leadership transition. If book-to-bill prints below 1.0 for a third consecutive quarter, the $2.8 billion backlog starts converting into visibly declining segment revenue in 2027 rather than a recovery, and the 0.90-times-revenue multiple we pay for that segment in the base case is too generous.

Third, the cost of the balance sheet. Interest expense ran at $20.4 million in the June quarter, an $82 million annual rate, and it is rising - net debt went from $1.008 billion to $1.386 billion in six months to fund the Quinnox purchase and buybacks. Leverage is about 3.5 times adjusted profit. The macro backdrop is hostile to that: the 30-year Treasury yield is 5.27%, the highest since 2007, the Federal Reserve held on 28-29 July with all three dissents voting FOR a hike, and roughly 57-65% odds of a September hike are priced with no cuts through December. Crucially, this thesis contains no rate-rescue leg and needs none - the revolver was refinanced and upsized to $600 million on 9 July 2026 with maturity pushed to 2031, so there is no wall to refinance into the storm. But every additional turn of leverage is now more expensive, and the first-half pattern of debt-funded acquisition plus buyback cannot repeat without impairing the equity.

What is NOT a hazard: cash burn. Free cash flow is positive and covers interest roughly 2.7 times.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic to exploit here, and that is part of why we are not paying up. The company pays no dividend, so there is no yield-focused holder base to flush on a cut. There is no index event: the shares remain a small-cap NYSE listing with no announced addition or deletion. There is no lock-up, no spin-off distribution and no announced secondary.

The flow that actually moved this stock ran the other way. The shares bottomed at $16.90 in July - roughly 69% below the 52-week high of $54.94 - which is the signature of a genuine capitulation in a thinly-covered small cap that had missed on margin, lost its federal bookings momentum and re-branded mid-stumble. That washout has already been harvested by whoever bought it. Since then the marginal buyer has been momentum and screen-driven: quantitative 'strong buy' value lists picked the name up on 31 July and again on 5 and 10 August, and the last week's 13% move came with no company news at all. The company itself has been buying, but at a decelerating pace - $46.0 million of repurchases in the September 2025 quarter, $64.2 million in December, $39.0 million in March, and only $11.5 million in June as cash went to the acquisition and to paying down borrowings. The corporate bid is thinner now than at any point in the last year, precisely when the price is highest.

The practical read: the shareholder base that would panic has already panicked, and the buyers who replaced it are price-insensitive on the way in and will be price-insensitive on the way out. A disappointing October print into a screen-driven holder base is a fast reversal, not an orderly de-rating.
moderator_conclusion:
We are continuing coverage, not opening it, and our call is unchanged: wait for the wash-out. A week ago at $28.44 we put base-case fair value at $36 and said the tension was that the market had already paid for the first proof point. The shares have since added another 13%, to $32.22, on no company news - an AWS partner-tier press release and two quantitative 'strong buy' list additions do not move intrinsic value. So the thesis is intact and the price has eaten most of it.

What we own an opinion on. Everforth is a real, cash-generative technology-services franchise, roughly 70% commercial and 30% federal, that has done genuine work converting itself from selling billable hours to selling delivered outcomes - consulting rose from 57% to about 63% of revenue and the 2025 margin path followed it up to 11%. The second-quarter print of 29 July confirmed the margin inflection was timing rather than breakage, with adjusted profit margin back to 9.6% and an earnings beat. Trailing free cash flow of $221 million against a $1.33 billion market value is a 17% yield, the revolver has been refinanced out to 2031, roughly 6% of the shares have been retired in a year, and insiders are buying in the open market. None of that is the signature of a business in terminal decline.

What stops us paying today's price. Three things, in order. First, the sum-of-the-parts arithmetic: on peer multiples we pulled live this morning, the parts come to about $36 in the base case, $22 in the adverse case and $50 in the favorable case. At $32.22 there is roughly ten dollars of downside against under four dollars of upside to fair value - the inverse of the setup we underwrote last week. Second, the leverage: net debt went from $1.008 billion to $1.386 billion in six months to fund an acquisition and buybacks while profit slipped, taking leverage from about 2.4 to about 3.5 times. Because debt is more than half of enterprise value, the equity absorbs the full force of any multiple compression - a 20% cut to the operating multiple takes roughly 40% off the share price. Third, and structurally, the federal segment's new-award book-to-bill has decayed for five straight quarters to 0.7 times with backlog down about 10%, and management has conceded on the record that its own artificial-intelligence accelerators complete work materially faster without any change in what it charges. Fewer billable hours at unchanged rates is revenue deflation with a lag, and it is why the whole commercial technology-services cohort has de-rated together. Everforth's 6.8 times profit is roughly in line with EPAM's 6.5 - the discount is sector-wide repricing, not a single-name mispricing, and we refuse to book shared sector beta as edge.

On the market backdrop: the current regime rewards catalysts with a calendar date and a cash payoff and penalises theses that need cheaper money. This one needs neither - the revolver is refinanced to 2031 and the thesis has no rate-cut leg, which is a genuine mark in its favour in a tape where the Federal Reserve is carrying a hiking bias and the 30-year yield is the highest since 2007. But it also has no live dated driver: the catalyst fired on 29 July, and the next scheduled event is a verification print in late October that is a hurdle, not a rescue.

On the two scores. Our execution call is 'wait', conviction 3 - the level we are waiting for is $26 or better, which restores roughly two dollars of upside for every dollar of risk against the same $36 base case; alternatively, we would move without a price concession on a single dated fact - federal trailing book-to-bill printing back above 1.0 in the October report. Separately, judging the value case alone with no catalyst overlay and no regime tilt: a business earning a 7.7% return on invested capital, below its cost of capital, with revenue down five consecutive years and earnings per share compounding down 12% a year, carries an eroding moat by this committee's own definition - and an eroding moat caps the value score at 3 regardless of the optical cheapness. With the discount to fair value now around a tenth, 3 is where it lands on its own merits anyway. A low multiple on a base that is shrinking is not value; it becomes value again at a price that pays us for the shrinkage, and $32.22 is not that price.
