A low multiple on a base that is shrinking is not value; it becomes value again at a price that pays us for the shrinkage, and $32.22 is not that price.

interrogator_dossier:
# Everforth, Inc. (NYSE: EFOR, formerly ASGN) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 2026-08-10. Transcript evidence: five consecutive quarterly calls, 2025-04-23 through 2026-04-22 (the company's first-quarter 2026 call was its last under the ASGN name). The 2026-07-29 second-quarter call is NOT in the transcript bundle; where I use second-quarter figures they come from the company's own results release of 29 July 2026 and from the filed statements, and I say so.*

*Price used throughout: $32.22 per share (US dollars, New York Stock Exchange), the live quote on 2026-08-10.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has changed shape three times in five quarters, and each shift moved the burden of proof further out in time.

**Spring 2025 — "resilience".** The first-quarter 2025 call is defensive in posture but calm in tone. Revenue of $968.3 million and an adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, as a percentage of revenue) of 9.7% were "in line with our guidance". The framing was stabilizers: "our business model demonstrates resilience across economic cycles, primarily due to our business stabilizers that support our gross margin, along with our variable cost structure." Two external shocks were named and quantified — tariffs and the federal cost-cutting programme known as DOGE. Management widened its guidance range and said so plainly: "there's a new piece of news almost daily here that all of our clients are reacting to."

**Mid-2025 to early 2026 — "mix shift".** Through the second, third and fourth quarters of 2025 the narrative turned offensive and settled on a single measurable claim: the company is converting itself from an information-technology staffing business into a consulting and solutions business. Consulting revenue rose from 57% of the total in early 2025 to roughly 63% by the fourth quarter. Adjusted margin climbed with it — 10.6%, then 11.1%, then 11.0%. Two acquisitions (TopBloc, a Workday services specialist, closed March 2025; Quinnox, an India-based digital-engineering firm, announced January 2026) were presented as the accelerant, alongside a $1 billion share-repurchase authorisation. This is the strongest stretch of the record: the claim was specific, the numbers moved with it, and management put capital behind it.

**Spring 2026 — "transformation, with a stumble".** The first-quarter 2026 call carries the rebrand to Everforth, a new stock ticker, a re-cut of segment reporting (from mode of delivery to industry vertical), three new segment presidents, and the closing of Quinnox. It also carries the first plain admission of a miss: "adjusted EBITDA margin of 8.6% was below our expectations for the quarter." Note what happened to the reporting change and the miss in the same call — the company stopped disclosing the staffing-versus-consulting split at exactly the moment its economics wobbled. The stated reason ("the delivery structure of our engagement is much less meaningful than the outcomes we drive") is defensible on the merits and convenient in its timing.

**Quietly dropped along the way:** the "business stabilizers" language of early 2025; the specific federal revenue baseline Ted Hanson volunteered in July 2025 ("mid $290 million to mid $295 million" per quarter); and, in the 2026 reporting change, the assignment-versus-consulting revenue disclosure that had been the transformation's own scoreboard.

**Newly introduced:** offshore delivery in India as a structural cost lever (Quinnox), proprietary artificial-intelligence "accelerators" as a differentiator, and the H-1B visa policy change reframed as "an incremental positive."

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where said | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our IT consulting revenues continue to grow… approximately 63% of revenues" | Q2–Q4 2025 | Consistent with a rising adjusted margin through 2025 (9.7% → 10.6% → 11.1% → 11.0%). But total revenue still fell: $4.45B (2023) → $4.10B (2024) → $3.98B (2025). | **Half true.** The mix is genuinely shifting; it has not yet arrested the top line. |
| "We're continuing to see our margins here kind of be creeping up" (on AI investment) | Q2 2025 | True through Q4 2025, then reversed: 8.6% in Q1 2026, 9.6% in Q2 2026 — both below the 2025 exit rate of 11.0%. | **Did not hold.** |
| "Our margins… it's not degrading, it's adding to our margin profile" | Q2 2025 | Net profit margin is 2.9% and earnings per share fell for the fifth consecutive year: $4.33 (2021) → $2.60 (2025), a five-year compound decline of about 12% a year. Trailing-twelve-month earnings per share are now $1.94. | **Contradicted by the trajectory.** |
| Federal business "positioned strongly for the future" on defence-budget growth | Q2–Q4 2025 | Federal new-award momentum decayed every quarter: book-to-bill (new bookings divided by revenue) on a trailing-twelve-month basis went 1.2x → 1.1x → 1.0x → 0.9x → **0.7x** by Q1 2026. Backlog fell from $3.1B to about $2.8B. | **Refuted by the company's own disclosure.** This is the single most damaging number in the record. |
| "Disciplined approach to capital allocation… without compromising the strength of our balance sheet" | Q4 2025 | Net debt (borrowings less cash) went from $1.008B at 31 Dec 2025 to $1.386B at 30 June 2026 — funding the $283.6M Quinnox purchase and roughly $50M of buybacks in the first half — while trailing adjusted profit fell from about $422M to about $400M. Leverage rose from roughly 2.4x to roughly **3.5x** in six months. | **Materially overstated.** Balance-sheet strength was spent, not preserved. |
| "We're not seeing a material compression in pricing" | Q1 2026 | Gross margin is stable (28.9%, and 28.3% in Q2 2026 versus 28.7% a year earlier). So the pricing claim survives; the damage is below the gross line — operating leverage, not price. | **Holds.** |
| Free cash flow "60% of our adjusted EBITDA converting" | Q1 2026 | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $221M on roughly $400M of adjusted profit — about 55%, close to the rule of thumb. | **Broadly holds.** |

The pattern: everything management says about *mix* and *cash conversion* checks out; everything it says about *the durability of margin and the balance sheet* has been overtaken by events.

One more forensic point the calls never surface. Shareholders' equity of $1.805B sits on top of $2.280B of goodwill and $0.596B of other intangible assets — tangible book value is roughly **negative $1.07B**. The screener's Altman-Z solvency score of 1.8 sits in the distress band. Neither is fatal for an asset-light services firm with $221M of free cash flow, but it means the equity is a claim on contracts and people, not on assets, and the debt is senior to all of it.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining, with a late partial recovery.**

- **Q1 2025 — cautious but composed.** "It's just the right thing to do here to widen the range." Management named its uncertainties and sized them ("we only expanded the range by $10 million on the top").
- **Q2 2025 — the high-water mark.** "Revenues of $1.02 billion were above the high-end of our guidance range." Confident, specific, forward-leaning: "we've got things developing here… we're on a path here that I think that we're going to be in a good spot."
- **Q3 2025 — confident, but the language turns abstract.** Heavy use of third-party validation (the ISG index) rather than first-party commitments: "AI spending is not merely a passing fad but a fundamental replatforming."
- **Q4 2025 — promotional.** The rebrand, the acquisition, the $1 billion authorisation and the Investor Day all arrive together. Superlatives multiply ("acquirer of choice", "record bookings").
- **Q1 2026 — the tone breaks.** "Below our expectations." Sales cycles "getting slightly longer as clients are deliberating longer before they pull the trigger." And the telling hedge, twice: "we will see the recovery in margin gradually throughout the year, won't rubber band it." When a management team pre-emptively tells you the recovery will be slow, it is managing an expectation it no longer controls.

The shift from offensive to defensive vocabulary is measurable: 2025 calls lead with bookings, wins and mix; the 2026 call leads with "disciplined expense management", "variability" and "volatile macro environment."

The 29 July 2026 second-quarter release (not in the transcript bundle) partially reverses this: adjusted earnings of $0.91 per share beat the $0.81 consensus, and adjusted margin recovered from 8.6% to 9.6%. But revenue of $1,007.0 million was still down about 1.3% from a year earlier, and reported net income of $14.2 million was down 52%.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium.**

Tracking each guide to its outcome:

| Guided in | For | Delivered | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025 (widened range) | Q2 2025 | $1.02B revenue "above the high-end"; margin 10.6% "at the top end" | Over-delivered |
| Q2 2025 | Q3 2025 | $1.01B and 11.1% — "both at the high end of our guidance ranges" | Delivered |
| Q3 2025 | Q4 2025 | $980.1M "at the top end"; 11.0% "exceeding our expectation" | Delivered |
| Q4 2025 | Q1 2026 | Revenue in range; **margin 8.6%, below expectations** | Missed |
| Q1 2026 | Q2 2026 | Revenue $1,007.0M; margin 9.6%; adjusted earnings $0.91 vs $0.81 expected | Beat |

That is a genuinely good record on revenue and a mixed one on margin. Two things stop it earning a High score.

First, the widened range of early 2025 was a lowered bar, and three "top of the range" quarters were cleared against it — the screener's beat rate of four in seven quarters (57%) is the unflattering long-run version. Second, and more importantly, the Q1 2026 miss came *directly after* record fourth-quarter bookings, and management's explanation was conversion timing: "our guide for Q1 assumed historical conversion of those things… the ramp-up time for those projects was slower than anticipated." A company that cannot forecast the conversion of its own signed backlog one quarter out has a real forecasting problem, not a macro problem.

No sandbagging pattern is evident; if anything the Q1 2026 guide was set too optimistically off the bookings number.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The margin run-rate.** Surinder Thind has pressed on it every call. In Q1 2025 he extracted a direct commitment — "so 2Q should be kind of the average run rate going forward… ?" and CFO Marie Perry answered "Yes." Margin has since ranged from 8.6% to 11.1%. In Q3 2025 he pushed again on the federal cost-reimbursable mix and got a deflection ("just the natural ebb and flow of certain contracts ending").

**The pricing of AI productivity — the question management keeps not answering.** In Q3 2025 Maggie Nolan asked whether accelerators that deliver work "25% faster" trigger a pricing conversation. Shiv Iyer: "We are exploring those opportunities, but we're not seeing a big uptick today." In Q1 2026 Mark Marcon asked the same question from the other side and got "we're not seeing a material compression in pricing." Both answers can be true at once and together they describe the core economic risk: the company is delivering the same outcome with fewer billable hours and is not being paid for the efficiency. In a business that sells hours, that is revenue deflation with a lag.

**Federal award velocity.** Analysts asked about DOGE's effect on decision-making from Q1 2025 onward. Rand Blazer's answer — "that velocity is less visible to us… of course, that's where we wouldn't be privy to that at any rate" — was honest and, in hindsight, a warning. The book-to-bill decay to 0.7x is that warning arriving.

**Not being asked, and it should be:** how a company adding leverage to buy growth (Quinnox) and to buy its own stock reconciles that with a shrinking federal backlog and a margin that has not returned to its 2025 exit rate.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Federal new-award collapse.** Trailing book-to-bill 1.2x (Q1 2025) → 0.7x (Q1 2026); backlog $3.1B → $2.8B. Roughly 30% of revenue is being fed by a shrinking pipeline.

🔴 **Leverage bought with a falling profit base.** Net debt $1.008B → $1.386B in six months while trailing adjusted profit slipped; leverage roughly 2.4x → 3.5x. Interest expense is now running at about $82M a year annualised from the second quarter.

🔴 **Five straight years of falling earnings.** $4.33 (2021) → $2.60 (2025) → $1.94 trailing. Revenue peaked in 2022 at $4.58B.

🔴 **Disclosure narrowed at the moment of the stumble** (Q1 2026): the staffing-versus-consulting split was retired in the same call that reported the first margin miss.

🔴 **Bookings that do not convert on schedule** (Q1 2026), following "record" fourth-quarter bookings (Q4 2025) — the transformation's own scoreboard proved a poor leading indicator.

🟢 **The mix shift is real and margin-accretive.** Consulting 57% → 63% of revenue; the 2025 margin path (9.7% → 11.0%) tracked it.

🟢 **Cash generation holds through the downturn.** $221M of trailing free cash flow on a $1.33B equity market value; conversion near the 60%-of-adjusted-profit rule of thumb.

🟢 **Second-quarter 2026 margin inflection** (29 July 2026): 8.6% → 9.6%, with an earnings beat — the first evidence the Q1 stumble was timing, as management claimed.

🟢 **Financing risk pushed out.** On 9 July 2026 the company refinanced and upsized its revolving credit facility to $600 million, extending maturity from 2028 to 2031. There is no near-term maturity wall.

🟢 **Shares are actually being retired.** Diluted share count 44.0M (Q1 2025) → 41.2M (Q2 2026), about 6% in a year, against a $1 billion authorisation.

🟢 **Insiders buying with their own money.** Open-market activity of 17 purchases (96,375 shares) against 11 sales (39,663 shares).

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**"Assets and accelerators" replaced "resources".** Across 2025 the unit of value being sold shifts in management's own vocabulary from people to intellectual property. Iyer floats productising it — "we have something called Pathfinder, which is an AI-driven cybersecurity product… conversations about pricing differently. But those are still early days" (Q3 2025). Early days, still, three quarters later.

**Offshore became strategy, not supplement.** In Q4 2025 Quinnox's India centres are described as "the foundation of our offshore delivery platform" with "EBITDA margins in the twenties" — roughly double the parent's. Management is buying the cost structure it cannot build. That is rational, and it is also an admission about the economics of the legacy base.

**Three new segment presidents in one quarter** (Q1 2026: Commercial North America, India and International, Federal Government). A wholesale operating-leadership replacement alongside a rebrand is a bigger vote of no confidence in the prior structure than the calm narration suggests.

**Competitive framing softened.** In Q3 2025 Iyer names the competitive set — "a combination of Accenture or the Big Four, in some cases, the India-based pure plays" — and insists "we're seeing pricing… really hold up." By Q1 2026 the competitive discussion has disappeared, replaced by client-deliberation language.

**A quiet compensation tell.** Asked in Q1 2026 whether sales incentives are being restructured for the consulting pivot, Ted Hanson describes "a normal amount of change" and Iyer adds "a core tenet of that plan hasn't shifted." A company genuinely re-engineering what it sells usually re-engineers how it pays for selling.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** This is not a stable compounder and it is not yet a broken business. It is a mid-cap technology-services firm midway through a deliberate conversion from selling billable hours to selling delivered outcomes — with a real, measurable mix shift behind it, and a shrinking revenue base, a compressed margin and a leveraged balance sheet in front of it.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** The federal segment, roughly 30% of revenue, has a trailing book-to-bill of 0.7x and a backlog down about 10% year on year. Everything bullish about this company rests on the commercial consulting side compounding fast enough to outrun that. Size the position to the possibility that it does not — and note that the entry price has already moved: the shares are $32.22 today against a low of $16.90 within the last year and a 50-day average of $21.06.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is genuine but thin — switching costs on multi-year engagements and embedded client relationships on the commercial side, plus a regulatory-licence element on the federal side (security clearances, contract vehicles, a $2.8B backlog that competitors cannot bid into mid-term). The evidence forces the "eroding" label rather than "narrow but stable": return on invested capital is 7.7%, below any plausible cost of capital, and falling; return on equity 12.8%; net margin 2.9%; the screener puts the current margin 2.5 standard deviations below its own historical peak; and earnings per share have compounded *down* 12% a year for five years. A business earning below its cost of capital on a shrinking revenue base does not have a widening moat, whatever the mix shift says.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The force is the automation of information-technology services labour — artificial intelligence decoupling revenue from headcount in a business model that bills hours at a spread. Management has already conceded the mechanism on the record: accelerators deliver discovery "25% faster" and capture "40% more" of requirements, and pricing has not changed to capture it. Fewer hours at unchanged rates is deflation. Two things keep it short of terminal. First, the federal 30% is protected by clearances and procurement friction that AI does not dissolve. Second, the company is on the delivering side of the same wave — the demand for the cloud, data and platform work that makes enterprise AI possible is real and is what carried the commercial book-to-bill at 1.1–1.2x through the downturn.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Neither cleanly, and that is the honest answer. At $32.22 the shares are about 6.0 times trailing free cash flow of $221M on the equity, and the whole enterprise (equity plus $1.386B of net debt) is about 6.8 times trailing adjusted profit — cheap in absolute terms and roughly *in line with*, not at a discount to, where the market now prices comparable commercial technology-services firms after their own de-rating. The cheapness is substantially a sector repricing, not a single-name mispricing. What tips it away from being a trap is the cash: $221M of annual free cash flow against a $1.33B market value, a refinanced revolver running to 2031, a shrinking share count and insiders buying. What keeps it away from being a bargain is the leverage at 3.5 times profit, the federal bookings hole, and the fact that the shares have already nearly doubled off the July low before any of it is proven.

---

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a moat that is being eroded · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.

bull_thesis:
Everforth (the renamed ASGN) is a cash-generative technology-services business, about 70% commercial and 30% U.S. federal, that the market priced in July 2026 as if its earnings were about to stop. The second-quarter result of 29 July 2026 said otherwise: revenue of $1,007 million beat the top of guidance, adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA - earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization - as a share of revenue) recovered from 8.6% in the March quarter to 9.6%, and adjusted earnings of $0.91 a share beat the $0.82 expected. Management's explanation for the March miss - record fourth-quarter bookings ramping more slowly, not prices breaking - now has a quarter of support.

The mix shift is real. Consulting rose from 57% to about 63% of revenue through 2025 and margin tracked it (10.6%, 11.1%, 11.0% in Q2-Q4 2025). Commercial consulting book-to-bill (new bookings divided by revenue) is 1.2 times on a trailing twelve-month basis, Workday bookings ran ahead of plan, and all five commercial industries grew sequentially in Q2 2026 - 'the most broad-based move forward that we've seen in a number of years'. Quinnox adds India delivery at gross margins of 40% or more. Transformation costs are falling ($12.8 million in Q1, $9.8 million in Q2, $7.5-9.5 million guided for Q3), which lifts reported margin mechanically.

Cash is the anchor: trailing free cash flow of $221 million against a $1.54 billion market value is a free-cash-flow yield of about 14%. Insiders have bought in the open market (17 buys against 11 sells). If margin returns to 11% on roughly $4.1 billion of revenue and the federal award engine recovers under its new leadership, the favourable sum-of-the-parts reaches about $52 a share.
bear_thesis:
Revenue peaked at $4.58 billion in 2022 and has fallen every year since to $3.98 billion in 2025; earnings per share fell from $5.23 to $2.60 and are $1.94 on a trailing basis. Return on invested capital of 7.7% is below any sensible cost of capital - a shrinking business earning less than its funding cost.

The federal half of the story is not recovering yet. Trailing federal book-to-bill ran 1.1x, 1.0x, 0.9x, 0.7x and 0.8x across the last five quarters and backlog fell from $3.1 billion (Q3 2025) to $2.7 billion (Q2 2026). Management's answer to direct questions on this was qualitative.

The balance sheet worsened to fund growth: net debt rose from about $1.01 billion at end-2025 to about $1.29 billion at 30 June 2026 after the $283.6 million Quinnox purchase, roughly 3.2 times adjusted profit, while buybacks slowed to $11.5 million in the June quarter. With net debt near half of enterprise value, a modest cut to the operating multiple takes a large bite out of the equity.

Structurally, AI tooling compresses billable hours in application development and staffing - the very work that built this company - and the company stopped disclosing its staffing-versus-consulting split in the quarter its margins missed. And the price: at $37.50 the shares have more than doubled from the $16.90 July low and now trade at our base-case fair value, so the re-rating the bull case describes has already been paid for.
consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable earnings power. It was in July at $16.90; at $37.50 it no longer is. The Street's published view is thin and stale: only one price target printed last quarter (Tobey Sommer, $36.00 on 22 July 2026, set when the stock was $18.31), the consensus target is $32.80 and the high $38.00 - the shares now trade above the consensus and near the highest target. Where we disagree with the bulls: today's price extrapolates one margin quarter (8.6% to 9.6%) into a full return to 11% while the federal pipeline is still shrinking. Where we disagree with the bears: the company is not in terminal decline - free cash flow of $221 million is real and commercial bookings are healthy. Fairly valued, in short.
forcing_function: The one forcing event - the 29 July 2026 margin recovery - has already fired. What remains is the 28 October 2026 third-quarter result, a verification point: watch adjusted margin (needs 10% or better to keep the recovery path credible) and federal trailing book-to-bill (needs to move back toward 1.0). The $1 billion buyback authorization is the largest lever management controls, but it is discretionary and was throttled to $11.5 million in the June quarter while cash went to Quinnox and debt.
valley_of_death: No liquidity event is in sight - the revolver runs to 2031 and free cash flow covers interest comfortably - but three hazards sit in the next three to nine months. First, the third-quarter print on 28 October 2026 lands on a stock that has more than doubled; consensus wants $1.02 a share and continued margin progress, and management has warned the recovery 'won't rubber band'. Second, a fourth sub-1.0 federal book-to-bill would start turning the shrinking $2.7 billion backlog into visibly lower federal revenue in 2027. Third, about $1.29 billion of net debt at roughly 3.2 times adjusted profit in a backdrop of high long rates keeps interest a meaningful drag on equity earnings.
positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling mechanism to wait for: no dividend to cut, no index event, no lock-up, no spin-off. The genuine capitulation happened in July 2026 at $16.90 and has been harvested. Since then the marginal buyer has been momentum and quantitative value screens, and the last week's 9.5% rise came on no company news. The seller who could bring the price to our level is a sector-wide sell-off in IT services - the group has de-rated repeatedly on fears that AI shrinks billable hours - or a disappointing third-quarter print that reverses the momentum crowd.
moderator_conclusion:
Wait for a better price: we buy near $32, which a sector-wide sell-off in IT services could deliver.

We are continuing coverage and our answer is unchanged from 5 October: the thesis holds and the price is the problem. Everforth is a real, cash-generative technology-services business - about $221 million of trailing free cash flow, an adjusted margin that recovered to 9.6% in the June quarter, and healthy commercial consulting bookings. But the moat is eroding (returns of 7.7%, five years of falling earnings), AI is a material threat to hours-based work, net debt is about $1.29 billion, and federal awards are still lagging. Our base-case sum-of-the-parts is $38.40 a share against an adverse case of $24.40 and a favourable case of $52.40.

At $37.50 the shares sit at fair value after rising about 9.5% in a week with no company news. In the current backdrop we need at least a 20% discount to fair value before buying, which puts our level at about $32. The 28 October 2026 third-quarter result is the next dated fact; if it confirms margin progress toward 11% and federal awards recovering, we would revisit fair value on that evidence rather than on the price.
sop_breakdown: Base case: Commercial Business $2.79 billion of revenue at 0.65 times = $1.81 billion; Federal Government Business $1.19 billion at 0.90 times = $1.07 billion; enterprise value about $2.89 billion; less net debt of about $1.285 billion (30 June 2026 balance sheet, borrowings $1.438 billion minus cash $152.9 million, ex-lease); equity about $1.6 billion over about 41.2 million diluted shares = about $38.40 a share. Sanity checks: that is about 7.2 times trailing adjusted profit of roughly $400 million and 0.73 times revenue on the whole company - in line with commercial IT-services peers checked live on 10 August 2026 (EPAM about 6.5 times profit and 0.79 times revenue, Genpact about 7.5 and 1.27) and below federal services peers (SAIC about 10.8, Booz Allen about 10.2). On the equity it is about 7 times trailing free cash flow of $221 million. The figure is unchanged from our 5 October look; we have not raised it to chase the price.
risk_reward: Unattractive at $37.50. The base case of $38.40 sits barely above the price, while the adverse case of $24.40 sits well below it; only the favourable case of $52.40 pays, and it needs both an 11% margin and a federal award recovery that are not yet in evidence. Net debt near half of enterprise value amplifies any multiple compression. The pipeline computes the ratios from these levels.
peer_comps_note: The supplied peer file for this ticker is unmapped (no peers, no anchor multiple), so we do not lean on a file multiple. Our own check, carried from live multiples pulled 10 August 2026: commercial IT services (EPAM about 6.5 times adjusted profit and 0.79 times revenue, Genpact 7.5 and 1.27) and federal services (SAIC 10.8 and 1.09, Booz Allen 10.2 and 1.15, CACI 17.7 and 2.03). At $37.50 Everforth trades at roughly 7.2 times trailing adjusted profit on the whole company - in line with the commercial cohort, and EPAM carries net cash where Everforth carries about 3.2 times leverage. The only apparent cheapness comes from putting federal multiples on the 30% federal slice, whose own awards are lagging peers. The commercial cohort's de-rating is a shared sector move on one unresolved driver - whether AI deflates hours-based services revenue - so any gap to other sectors is sector beta, not name-specific edge.
interrogator_dossier:
# Everforth (EFOR, formerly ASGN) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Prepared 2026-10-12 from five earnings calls (2025-07-23 through 2026-07-29) and the screener's financial trajectory. Live price used: $37.50 (NYSE, USD, FMP quote 2026-10-12). Next print: third quarter 2026, scheduled 2026-10-28 (consensus $1.02 adjusted earnings per share on about $1,011 million of revenue).

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has moved in three steps. In mid-2025 (Q2 2025 call, 2025-07-23) ASGN described itself as an IT staffing and consulting hybrid whose consulting share was rising - "approximately 63% of revenues ... up from 57% in the year-ago period" - with the federal business pitched as a beneficiary of the One Big Beautiful Bill defense budget. By the Investor Day (November 2025) and the Q4 2025 call (2026-02-04) the frame became a "next wave growth strategy" toward "higher value, higher margin, technology and digital engineering solutions", backed by the Quinnox purchase (India offshore delivery) and a $1 billion buyback authorization. By Q1 2026 (2026-04-22) the company renamed itself Everforth and stopped reporting commercial revenue by delivery mode (staffing versus consulting) in favour of industry and solution lenses. In Q2 2026 (2026-07-29) the narrative became explicitly about AI: "the last mile of enterprise AI adoption will be execution through IT services."

What was quietly dropped: the staffing-versus-consulting revenue split, the cleanest metric investors had for tracking the mix shift. Dropping it in the same quarter that margins missed is the single most notable disclosure change in the window.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (quarter) | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Consulting mix rising drives margin (Q2-Q4 2025) | Adjusted margin 10.6%, 11.1%, 11.0% across Q2-Q4 2025 as consulting reached ~63% | Matches |
| Record Q4 bookings would convert in Q1 (Q4 2025) | Q1 2026 margin 8.6%, below guide; earnings $0.69 vs $0.98 expected | Missed - management blamed slower ramp |
| Margin recovery gradual, "won't rubber band" (Q1 2026) | Q2 2026 margin 9.6%, above the top of guide; earnings $0.91 vs $0.82 expected | Delivered, one quarter |
| Federal defense budget is a tailwind (Q2 2025 onward) | Federal trailing book-to-bill 1.1x, 1.0x, 0.9x, 0.7x, 0.8x; backlog $2.9bn to $3.1bn then down to $2.7bn | Diverges - the tailwind has not shown up in awards |
| Growth strategy | Revenue $4.58bn (2022) to $3.98bn (2025); earnings per share $5.23 to $2.60; trailing $1.94 | The story is far richer than the trajectory |
| Disciplined balance sheet (Q4 2025) | Net debt about $1.01bn at 2025-12-31 to about $1.29bn at 2026-06-30 (cash $152.9m per the Q2 release) after the $283.6m Quinnox buy | Leverage rose, roughly 3.2x adjusted profit |
| Cash generation | Trailing free cash flow $221m; management guides ~60% of adjusted profit converting | Corroborated - the strongest part of the case |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: Stable, turning slightly more confident in the latest call. Q2 2025 and Q3 2025 were confident and specific ("solid performance ... at the high end of our guidance ranges"). Q4 2025 was offensive - acquisition, rebrand, buyback. Q1 2026 turned defensive: "a very volatile macro environment", "sales cycles are getting slightly longer", recovery "not a rubber band". Q2 2026 recovered: "the most broad-based move forward that we've seen in a number of years", all five commercial industries up sequentially, commercial expected back to year-on-year growth "in the fourth quarter for sure". Guidance specificity stayed consistent throughout.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Four of the last five quarters landed at or above the top of the guide; Q1 2026 margin missed badly. The screener's beat rate of 4 of 7 quarters (57%) is consistent with a management that guides carefully but not conservatively. No sandbagging pattern. Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- Federal book-to-bill: Tobey Sommer (Q2 2026) pushed for "brute force metrics" to drive better book-to-bill; the answer was qualitative ("submitted waiting award numbers ... up materially"), no figure.
- Quinnox contribution: Mark Marcon asked directly; management declined to break it out ("we didn't call out the Quinnox numbers"), only that growth was "mostly organic".
- Gross margin: Marcon established that year-on-year commercial gross margin compression came from permanent-placement weakness and the Mexican peso, and that the Q2 guide gap came from more low-margin cost-plus federal work.
- AI displacement of hours-based work and pricing of accelerators (Maggie Nolan, Q3 2025): management admits it is exploring outcome pricing but "not seeing a big uptick today".
